title: America's Demoralized Men, Part II: Lost Pathways, Greater Struggles | Institute for Family Studies
gist: A YouGov survey of 2,000 US men ages 18-29 (fielded April 2025) finds roughly half report chronic loneliness or lack of community, 42% think they are failures, 61% feel little control over their lives, and 72% believe connections beat merit — while daily gambling (23%), daily porn (27%) and near-constant gaming (44%) are widespread and correlate with distress. The authors argue the driver is 'deinstitutionalization' — the loss of prescribed pathways (college, trade, church, marriage, stable employer) — not individual laziness or toxic masculinity, and note young men are 'alienated from the system but optimistic about themselves.'

insights.claim: In a nationally representative April 2025 YouGov survey of 2,000 US men ages 18-29, 25% report feeling lonely and 26% isolated all or most of the time in the prior 30 days, and 20% seldom or never feel loved or wanted.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Quantifies the addressable market for loneliness-adjacent products (community apps, men's mental health, third places) at roughly a quarter of the 18-29 male cohort in acute need, half in partial need.
insights.quote: the bad news is that a substantial portion of our respondents report feeling lonely (25%) or isolated (26%) all or most of the time in the past 30 days
insights.locator: If the good news is that half

insights.claim: The authors reject 'epidemic' framing for male loneliness: a meta-analysis of hundreds of UCLA Loneliness Scale studies since the mid-1970s shows loneliness among 18-29 year olds rising linearly for half a century, meaning this is a slow structural trend, not a post-COVID or post-smartphone shock.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Trend-not-shock framing means loneliness-driven demand is secular and durable rather than a fad reversing as memory of the pandemic fades — but also that no single intervention or policy catalyst will inflect it.
insights.quote: “Epidemic,” however, is not the right word because this dire situation did not arise suddenly.
insights.locator: “Epidemic,” however, is not the right

insights.claim: The much-cited 'male friendship recession' statistic is not male-specific: the same 2024 dataset shows 17% of men and 16% of women report no close friend, so young men are not the social outlier the discourse claims.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Products and policy pitched narrowly at 'male loneliness' may be mis-segmenting a market that is roughly gender-symmetric; the addressable population is far larger than the male framing implies.
insights.quote: In fact, men and women look practically the same in this dataset, with 17 percent of men and 16 percent of women reporting that they ‘do not have a close friend.’
insights.locator: 17 percent of all Americans had no close friends

insights.claim: Marriage sharply reduces but does not eliminate loneliness — 67% of married men versus 41% of unmarried men report rarely feeling lonely, yet 14% of married young men still feel lonely all or most of the time.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that family formation alone solves male distress; 1 in 7 married young men remains acutely lonely, meaning the market for connection services extends into the 'settled' demographic.
insights.quote: if we just focus on the married men alone, apart from any comparisons, we find that 14% say they have felt lonely all or most of the time
insights.locator: For example, in our survey, a much higher percentage

insights.claim: College enrollment is a loneliness risk factor, not a protective one: 28% of men currently in school feel lonely all or most of the time versus 16% of non-students holding a bachelor's degree, and a spring 2025 survey found 46% of undergraduate men screened positive for loneliness on the UCLA scale.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Campus mental-health demand is concentrated during enrollment while the payoff comes after graduation — relevant to university service budgets, student wellness vendors, and retention risk.
insights.quote: those in school (including 2- and 4-year colleges, trade schools, and apprenticeship programs) are much more likely to report feeling lonely all or most of the time (28%) than non-students with a bachelor’s degree (16%)
insights.locator: For many, the college years can be

insights.claim: 42% of young men report two or fewer close friends, including 9% with none, and the deficit spans every subgroup — 31% of husbands, 36% of fathers, 31% of college graduates, 32% of religious men, and about 40% of both liberals and conservatives.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: No demographic segment can be written off as 'already served' — the friendship gap is universal, which widens the total addressable market but eliminates easy targeting shortcuts.
insights.quote: No demographic group is immune to the lack of friendships.
insights.locator: For many young men, there is clearly a substantial friendship deficit

insights.claim: Participation in all-male groups during childhood or adolescence — sports teams, Boy Scouts — raises the odds of having three or more close friends in adulthood by 16 percentage points (64% vs 48%) and cuts the odds of having zero friends by 9 points (5% vs 14%).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A concrete, cheap, replicable intervention with lasting adult effects — supports the investment case for youth sports infrastructure, scouting-type organizations, and boys' programming.
insights.quote: his chance of having three or more friends (64%) was some 16 percentage points higher than those who said no (48%), and his chance of having no friends was about 9 percentage points lower (5% vs. 14%)
insights.locator: Another factor that contributes to more friendships

insights.claim: Friendship count does not reliably buy belonging: 21% of men with three to five close friends and 20% of those with six or more still report feeling isolated, and the 25% who feel chronically lonely far exceeds the 9% who report zero friends.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Subjective belonging and objective social contact are separate variables — solutions that only add contacts (apps, meetups, matching) will underdeliver on the emotional outcome buyers actually want.
insights.quote: Friendships help but do not guarantee feeling included.
insights.locator: While friendship is certainly a protective factor

insights.claim: 48% of young men agree they do not belong to anything they would call a community (18% strongly, 30% somewhat), including 36% of religious men, 36% of bachelor's degree holders, and 28% of married men with kids.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Community deficit is not confined to the disconnected tail — even the most institutionally embedded third of the cohort reports it, suggesting the supply of belonging has shrunk economy-wide.
insights.quote: 18% strongly agree that they have no community they can call their own, with an additional 30% agreeing somewhat
insights.locator: As with the loneliness and isolation questions

insights.claim: 53% of US men ages 18-29 are effectively secular (39% never attend religious services, 14% attend less than once a year), 23% are nominal, and only 25% attend more than monthly.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The addressable congregation among young men has fallen to a quarter of the cohort — a direct headwind to church finances, faith-based media, and religiously-anchored civic infrastructure.
insights.quote: This is the group we label “secular,” and it includes more than half of all young men (53%).
insights.locator: What is striking here is just how few

insights.claim: Religiosity is the single strongest correlate of civic participation — 81% of religious men participate in at least one activity versus 66% of nominal and 42% of secular men, and religious men volunteer at roughly double the secular rate (45% vs 22%) — but secular men outnumber religious ones by more than two to one.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Putnam's transmission channel is intact but the input has collapsed: any forecast of volunteer labor supply for nonprofits, disaster response, or youth programs should be discounted by the 2:1 secular tilt.
insights.quote: The problem, from the Putnam perspective, is that the secular contingent outnumbers the religious by more than two to one.
insights.locator: In our survey, we find that religious respondents

insights.claim: Reports of a young-male religious revival are offset by equal defection: 28% say they have become more religious in recent years but 26% say less religious, with the gains concentrated among men who already attend regularly (52% of the religious group) and losses concentrated among the nominal (29%) and secular (32%).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The 'young men returning to church' narrative is intensification among the already-committed, not conversion — so expect deepening engagement per member rather than growth in the member base.
insights.quote: However, a similar percentage of respondents (26%) report a decline in religiosity, including among the nominal (29%) and secular (32%).
insights.locator: A question much discussed in recent years

insights.claim: 72% of young men agree that who you know matters more than ability or hard work in getting ahead (27% strongly, 45% somewhat), with only 7% strongly disagreeing — and the belief shows almost no variation by employment, parenthood, age, education or family intactness.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A near-consensus anti-meritocratic belief that survives even among the successful is a leading indicator for political realignment, populist policy demand, and declining willingness to invest in credentials.
insights.quote: the primacy of “who you know” is clearly a widely shared conviction about the economic system, indivisible by the categories where we typically find differences
insights.locator: Nearly three-quarters of young men

insights.claim: About half of young men (19% strongly, 30% somewhat) agree that no matter how hard they work, people like them will never achieve the American Dream — including 43% of full-time and self-employed men, 60% of the non-working, and 36% of those holding a bachelor's degree or higher.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Even the employed and credentialed have priced in mobility failure, which supports persistent demand for lottery-like wealth routes and weakens the political constituency for status-quo economic policy.
insights.quote: many young men believe that current economic realities deny people like them the chance to attain a better and more secure future
insights.locator: Half of young men strongly (19%)

insights.claim: The report argues young men's gambling and day-trading, not steady employment, is now the expressed mechanism by which they expect to realize their opportunities, and notes economists have started calling this a 'casino economy.'
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Directly bullish structural demand for sportsbooks, prediction markets, and retail brokerage among young men — and it frames that demand as a substitute for wage income, meaning it is countercyclical to labor market hope, not to income.
insights.quote: how they expect to realize them might be better indicated by their extensive gambling and day-trading than by steady work in a 9-5 job. Even economists have taken to referring to the current situation as a “casino economy.”
insights.locator: This is not the old job market

insights.claim: Half of college graduates in the survey doubt their education was worth the time or money, undermining the credential as a mobility product even among those who completed it.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Direct demand risk for four-year enrollment, tuition pricing power, and student lending — the buyers who completed the purchase are unwilling advocates for it.
insights.quote: Even half of college graduates doubt that their education was worth the time or money.
insights.locator: We find that many young men do not see

insights.claim: 61% of young men say the statement 'I often feel that I have little control over the things that happen to me' describes them very (21%) or somewhat (40%) well, with only 1 in 10 fully rejecting it; among the non-working (not students or caregivers) the figure rises to 72% versus 53% of the full-time employed.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Low self-mastery is the psychological precondition for both gambling behavior and labor-force exit — a variable to watch as a leading indicator for both.
insights.quote: a remarkable 61% of young men say very (21%) or somewhat (40%) well
insights.locator: To explore further, we presented two statements

insights.claim: 42% of young men agree that 'all in all, I am inclined to think that I am a failure' describes them (15% very well, 27% somewhat well), and only 1 in 3 fully reject it; the rate reaches 56% among men neither working nor in school and 47% among those without and not pursuing a degree.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Self-assessed failure at four in ten is the core 'demoralization' metric the whole report is built on — the single number to track across future waves.
insights.quote: More than 4 in 10 young men feel this statement describes them “very well” (15%) or “somewhat well” (27%); only 1 in 3 fully reject it.
insights.locator: The second statement, also phrased negatively

insights.claim: Trade school and apprenticeship graduates match college graduates on most outcomes but break the pattern on self-worth — 49% see themselves as failures, close to the 46% of men without degrees — and 88% of them feel people underestimate their potential, the highest of any group.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Status stigma, not economic outcome, is the binding constraint on skilled-trades recruitment — a marketing and cultural problem, and a lever for anyone trying to fill the trades pipeline.
insights.quote: here, the outcomes for trade school or apprenticeship graduates, with 49% seeing themselves as failures, are much closer to those without degrees (46%)
insights.locator: In this report, we have repeatedly observed

insights.claim: Despite pervasive fatalism about the system, personal optimism is intact and high: 84% say they have ambitious goals for their future, 81% say they can do anything they set their mind to, and 75% expect greater opportunities than their parents had.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Contradicts the 'checked out, nihilistic young men' consensus — this cohort is still spending, striving and buying aspiration, which matters for consumer and education marketing.
insights.quote: But that is not what we found—not even close.
insights.locator: But that is not what we found

insights.claim: The report's central formulation is that young men are 'alienated from the system but optimistic about themselves' — they have abandoned belief in meritocracy while retaining faith in their own powers.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for reading young-male behavior: expect anti-institutional politics and consumption paired with individualistic risk-taking (crypto, betting, solo entrepreneurship), not withdrawal.
insights.quote: They are, we might say, alienated from the system but optimistic about themselves.
insights.locator: Alternatively, while many young men may have lost faith

insights.claim: 45% of young men report having experienced depression, anxiety or bipolar disorder, with 29% currently experiencing symptoms or in treatment; 37% report depression (21% current), 33% anxiety (21% current), and 16% bipolar disorder (8% currently treated).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Reported prevalence runs above epidemiological estimates for this cohort — sizes the behavioral-health services and psychiatric-drug market for young men, while flagging self-report inflation as a caveat.
insights.quote: when the three disorders are grouped together, we find that 45% of our respondents have experienced at least one of them, and 29% are currently doing so
insights.locator: Depression and anxiety disorders are even more commonly

insights.claim: 35% of young men took a prescription medication for mental or emotional health in the past 12 months, and 12% are taking one daily.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: One in three young men is an active psychiatric-pharma customer within a year — a concrete volume anchor for SSRI/ADHD/mood-drug demand and telehealth prescribing platforms.
insights.quote: We find that 1 in 3 (35%) young men have taken a medication in that time period, with 12% currently doing so on a daily basis.
insights.locator: Among possible treatments, we asked all respondents

insights.claim: 44% of young men have experienced at least one potentially traumatic event: 28% have had a loved one go to prison, 18% a loved one die of drug overdose, 16% a loved one die by suicide, and 14% know someone killed by homicide; separately, 12% have themselves been incarcerated.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The deaths-of-despair and mass-incarceration eras have left a measurable trauma footprint across nearly half of an entire male birth cohort — a durable driver of health, justice and social-service costs.
insights.quote: An extraordinary 44% of young men report experiencing at least one of these stressful events.
insights.locator: In addition to the stressful circumstances discussed above

insights.claim: Trauma exposure roughly doubles mental-health diagnosis rates across the board — depression 49% vs 27%, anxiety 44% vs 25%, ADHD 36% vs 19%, learning disability 21% vs 11% — and more than triples bipolar disorder (26% vs 8%); incarceration rates run 22% vs 4%.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Trauma history is the highest-yield single screening variable for identifying the acutely distressed subgroup — useful for triage, targeting, and understanding which men drive aggregate distress statistics.
insights.quote: In the case of bipolar disorder, they are more than three times as likely.
insights.locator: In the figure below, we can see a clear association

insights.claim: Institutional embeddedness cuts current mental illness roughly in half: 41% of men neither working nor in school currently have anxiety, depression or bipolar disorder versus 21% of the full-time employed; married fathers are at 16% versus 31% for both married-without-kids and unmarried-without-kids men; religious men 20% versus secular 32%; BA holders 18% versus 32% without.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Marriage-plus-children, regular religious attendance, and full-time work each associate with a ~50% reduction in current mental illness — the strongest 'protective bundle' identified in the data.
insights.quote: married men with kids are around half as likely (16%) to have current anxiety, bipolar disorder, or depression as those who are married without kids (31%) and those who are unmarried without kids (31%)
insights.locator: Like so many areas of analysis in this report

insights.claim: More than half of young men now gamble: 23% daily, 12% several times a week, and 21% weekly or less — with the highest daily rates among unmarried fathers (39%), current students (34%) and conservatives (32%).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Daily-gambler penetration of 23% among 18-29 men, concentrated in financially fragile segments, is both a revenue base for sportsbooks and the core exposure in any future regulatory crackdown.
insights.quote: In fact, more than half of young men in our survey are now gamblers.
insights.locator: Almost overnight, gambling, including sports and event betting

insights.claim: Around 2 in 3 regular online gamblers report at least some gambling-caused emotional distress, with roughly 1 in 10 characterizing distress and life problems as severe or extreme and another 29% as moderate.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Self-acknowledged harm at this scale is the raw material for litigation, state-level restriction, advertising bans and responsible-gaming mandates — a live regulatory tail risk for betting operators.
insights.quote: Around 1 in 10 young men characterize gambling-related distress and life problems as severe or extreme.
insights.locator: Respondent’s answers strongly suggest that activities like gambling

insights.claim: 43% of young men watch pornography daily (27%) or several times a week (16%), and daily use is not confined to the marginalized — it includes 21% of married men, 24% of regular religious service attenders, 23% of the full-time employed, and 32% of current students.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Breaks the stereotype that heavy porn use marks the dropout tail — usage is mainstream across employed, married and religious segments, which changes the political calculus of any age-verification or restriction regime.
insights.quote: we also find daily use among married men (21%), the regular religious service attenders (24%), those who hold full-time jobs (23%), and those currently in school (32%)
insights.locator: The prevalence of pornography use, the third concern

insights.claim: 66% of young men play video games at least once a day, with 44% playing many times a day or more, and only 5% never playing.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Near-universal daily engagement makes gaming the default attention substrate for this cohort — the channel through which any product, message or monetization reaches them.
insights.quote: An incredible 44% report playing many times a day or more, and another 22% report playing about “once a day.”
insights.locator: Finally, we turn to gaming habits

insights.claim: Gaming is doing substitute work for missing institutions: about 40% of frequent gamers say they play to interact with others or make friends, a similar share for a sense of mastery or accomplishment, nearly half as a way to temporarily escape real-life responsibilities, and over 25% for a chance to be someone different.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Games are monetizing unmet needs for friendship, mastery and identity — the durable moat for social and progression-driven titles, and the reason engagement is compulsive rather than discretionary.
insights.quote: the escaping doesn’t look so temporary when virtually every free moment is dedicated to playing
insights.locator: To be clear, the issue here is not with a pleasant pastime

insights.claim: Distress correlates with the transactional screen activities, not the ubiquitous ones: daily social media and gaming users report feeling like failures at about the same rate as light users, but 66% of daily gamblers and 63% of daily porn viewers do — versus 42% of men overall — with day trading and fantasy sports showing the same pattern.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Reframes the screen-harm debate away from social media and toward wagering and sexual content — a targeting signal for where regulation and litigation should be expected to land next.
insights.quote: those who view pornography (63%) and gamble (66%) every day—along with day trading and playing fantasy sports—are significantly more inclined to see themselves as a failure
insights.locator: Turning now to the question of consequences.

insights.claim: The report deliberately deprioritizes social media as a driver of male distress, arguing time spent gaming, gambling and viewing pornography matters far more, and noting the great majority of influencers are women.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Cuts against the dominant Haidt-style social-media-causes-harm narrative for young men specifically; if adopted, shifts regulatory attention and liability exposure from platforms to betting and adult-content operators.
insights.quote: we are of the view, with some research justification, that the amount of time that young men play video games or gamble or watch pornography is far more significant than social media consumption (where the great majority of influencers are women)
insights.locator: Maladaptive Coping With Screentime

themes.theme: Deinstitutionalization Thesis and the Trades Gap

insights.claim: The report's core thesis is deinstitutionalization: the sharp decline of prescribed roles, inherited life courses, and clear occupational and educational trajectories has replaced structure with 'a precarious freedom,' and this loss of form — not laziness or toxic masculinity — best explains young men's distress.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The reusable model: distress tracks distance from institutions (school, church, employer, marriage). Any product, policy or firm that re-supplies structure and defined pathways is selling into a real, growing deficit.
insights.quote: Where there was once a given social pattern, an “institution,” like sustained work for the same company, there is now a more open and indeterminate field of options and choices. A precarious freedom
insights.locator: Among the causal explanations, the structural argument

insights.claim: Completing an institutionalized pathway — college, trade school or apprenticeship — is the strongest observed predictor of good outcomes, but the benefit appears only after graduation, not during, when the experience is often lonely and distressing.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Completion, not enrollment, is what pays — which makes attrition the key metric for evaluating any education or workforce program, and explains why in-program satisfaction surveys mislead.
insights.quote: This benefit, incidentally, often does not appear while they were in college/training, which could be a lonely, distressing time.
insights.locator: We see what is lost by the importance of the college track

insights.claim: The non-college pipeline is essentially missing in the US: 15% have completed a trade or apprenticeship program with high employment, but schools still stress college-for-all, defined school-to-employer pipelines are absent, and the average age of a US apprentice is 29 — meaning men lose roughly a decade bouncing between entry-level jobs.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A decade of lost human-capital accumulation per non-college man is the specific, quantified market gap for workforce-development firms, employer-sponsored training, and skilled-trades staffing.
insights.quote: Young men, not on the college track, often step into a void after high school, bouncing around entry-level jobs, and may only discover a vocation, such as a trade, much later. While varying somewhat by industry, the average age of an apprentice in the U.S. is 29.
insights.locator: But the higher education pathway is not open to many men

insights.claim: The report attributes stagnant or declining real wages for young men to offshoring of manufacturing, cheap migrant labor, and the elimination of private-sector labor unions, with volatility now compounded by gig work, new technologies, and the looming threat of AI-driven job loss.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The report treats AI job displacement as the next leg of a multi-decade male wage shock — if it lands, expect the demoralization metrics here to deteriorate rather than mean-revert.
insights.quote: Other shifts have increased the volatility of the economy, such as the rise of unstable gig work, the disruption of new technologies, and now the looming threat of job loss due to AI.
insights.locator: In the current economic environment, where work is now

insights.claim: Only 63% of young men had their biological father present continuously growing up (16% absent entirely, 21% intermittent), but 69% of those without a biological, adoptive or step father still had a father figure — most often an uncle or relative (30%), older brother (16%), teacher (15%), coach (12%) or a Big Brother-type mentor (8%).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The 'no male role models' framing is overstated — extended family and school/sport adults are filling the gap, which is where mentorship investment actually has leverage.
insights.quote: For the great majority of young men (69%) who grew up without a biological father, adoptive father, or stepdad, a father figure was present in their lives.
insights.locator: We also offered a write-in option

insights.claim: The report rejects the 'toxic masculinity' explanation on its own data: 73% of men say it has become harder to know what it is to be a man, but manosphere influencer Andrew Tate scored low marks, mothers (79%) and fathers (69%) top the role-model list, and over 85% define manhood as responsibility and sacrifice for others.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Undercuts the commercial and political premise that young men are being radicalized en masse by online masculinity influencers — the influence market may be far smaller than press coverage implies.
insights.quote: nothing in our data suggests that lots of young men are under undue influence from bad characters or clinging to views of masculinity that could be legitimately described as “toxic.”
insights.locator: We find that a large majority of men (73%)

insights.claim: The authors argue relationships were historically inherited through overlapping webs of association rather than individually built, quoting Pressler and Duggan that community 'has never been solely individual choices to make nor individual responsibilities to develop' — which is why self-help prescriptions to young men fail.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Explains why individual-level interventions (apps, advice, exhortation) underperform: the missing input is inherited associational infrastructure, which only institutions can supply.
insights.quote: Contrary to the self-help ethos that pervades our society, relationships and community have never been solely individual choices to make nor individual responsibilities to develop.
insights.locator: We inherit many overlapping webs of association
